answer: A karst conservation exchange pays agents for finding pollution leaks, but copying the same analysis kernel under many names should not multiply rewards. Each report must name a unique spring and sampling hour, include a lab-signed water sample, and lock a bond until an independent retest. The ledger pays once for a verified leak; aliases need distinct real samples and capital at risk. A juniper grove beside the spring may help locate it, but neither a photo nor a lab signature alone proves a new leak. Colluding labs can still fake samples, so random field visits remain necessary.
